Participants are shown squares on paper (base grids) that can be folded along the marked lines.
Two lines in the grid were highlighted (yellow) and participants were asked to evaluate whether these lines would overlap in the cube.
In the kinesthetic self-imagery condition, participants were instructed to focus on the feeling while they imagined folding the paper themselves.

In the visual object-imagery condition, participants were instructed to focus on visual aspects while they imagined that the paper is folded by itself (like an invisible magical hand), i.e., a no-person perspective from the outside (visual imagery without an actor).
In the kinesthetic self-imagery condition, participants were instructed to focus on the feeling while they imagined turning themselves into the depicted position and raising one's own limb.
In the visual object-imagery condition, participants were instructed to focus on visual aspects while they imagined the depicted figure to turn into one's own position and lowering the limb.
Some squares flashed yellow (700 ms) in a certain sequence, and the participants were asked to reproduce the same sequence by clicking on the respective squares.

All participants gave informed consent and received course credit for their participation.
Participants are shown squares on paper (base grids) that can be folded along the marked lines.
Two lines in the grid were highlighted (yellow) and participants were asked to evaluate whether these lines would overlap in the cube.
In the kinesthetic self-imagery condition, participants were instructed to focus on the feeling while they imagined folding the paper themselves.

In the visual object-imagery condition, participants were instructed to focus on visual aspects while they imagined that the paper is folded by itself (like an invisible magical hand), i.e., a no-person perspective from the outside (visual imagery without an actor).
In the kinesthetic self-imagery condition, participants were instructed to focus on the feeling while they imagined turning themselves into the depicted position and raising one's own limb.
In the visual object-imagery condition, participants were instructed to focus on visual aspects while they imagined the depicted figure to turn into one's own position and lowering the limb.
Some squares flashed yellow (700 ms) in a certain sequence, and the participants were asked to reproduce the same sequence by clicking on the respective squares.
Participants were required to press the 'x' key if the arrow indicated towards the left side and to press the 'm' key if the arrow indicated towards the right side.

text.text: While theoretical accounts of action imagery emphasize the role of the actor performing the movement, it remains unclear whether self-related kinesthetic imagery (selfimagery) compared to object-related visual imagery (object-imagery) supports mental transformations similarly for body-related and non-body stimuli.
To clarify this relationship, 142 participants completed the mental paper folding task and the mental body rotation task under two imagery instructions: based on self-imagery or objectimagery.
Instructions successfully shifted subjective imagery experiences, with selfimagery emphasizing bodily sensations and object-imagery emphasizing visualization.

Performance analyses revealed robust task-specific effects: mental paper folding performance decreased with the number of folds and direction changes, and mental body rotation performance decreased for larger (than smaller) rotations, for front-view (than back-view) stimuli and for foot (than hand) stimuli.
Crucially, errors did not significantly differ between imagery instructions.
For response times, however, the relative advantage of the instructions was task-specific.
Response times were shorter under self-imagery in mental body rotations but shorter under object-imagery in mental paper folding.
Yet, in mental paper folding, this effect varied with instruction order, which might reflect a carryover effect of self-referential processing from self-imagery to object-imagery.
Cross-task response times resulted in medium correlations when imagery instructions matched, whereas error rate correlations showed no consistent pattern.
Overall, the findings indicate that the advantage of self-imagery versus objectimagery depends on task demands.

They are consistent with flexible recruitment of imagery processes, while leaving open whether this reflects different configurations of a shared system or partly distinct motor and visuospatial strategies.

Mental imagery, the simulation of sensory experiences in the absence of direct perceptual input, plays a central role in a variety of cognitive and motor functions (Kosslyn et al., 1984; Thompson & Kosslyn, 2000).

text.text: Within motor cognition, action imagery (also referred to as action simulation or motor imagery; Moreno-Verdú et al., 2024) is commonly conceptualized as the internal simulation of an action "as if" executed by oneself, relying on motor representations that overlap with those involved in actual movement (Hétu et al., 2013; Jeannerod, 2001).

text.text: This raises a fundamental theoretical question of whether action imagery depends on representing oneself as the acting agent, or whether action-related transformations can also be performed from an object-centered perspective without an explicit self-actor (Callow et al., 2013; Dahm & Sachse, 2025).

text.text: This distinction is particularly relevant because self-performed imagery is typically accompanied by kinesthetic sensations, whereas object-centered imagery can emphasize visual representations of an action or its effects without representing an actor (Chholak et al., 2019; Cumming & Eaves, 2018; Guillot et al., 2009; Naito et al., 2002; Steggemann et al., 2011).

text.text: Embodied cognition provides a framework for reconciling these perspectives.
Bodily experience can constrain and shape action representations without requiring the self to be explicitly represented as the actor (Barsalou, 2010; Wilson, 2002).

text.text: Accordingly, action imagery may range from strongly embodied, kinesthetic simulations centered on one's own body to more visually dominated, object-centered simulations that track an action or its effects.

This distinction also corresponds to partially different sensory emphases: kinesthetic imagery is more consistently associated with motor and somatosensory processing, whereas visual imagery places greater demands on visuospatial transformation mechanisms (Guillot et al., 2009; Kilintari et al., 2016).

text.text: Importantly, these differences need not imply categorically separate imagery systems.

Instead, self-and object-imagery may represent different configurations within a partially shared imagery architecture, with the relative contribution of embodied and visuospatial processes depending on the actor represented and the task demands (Van Caenegem et al., 2024).

text.text: Consistent with this flexible account, recent evidence indicates that even the temporal dynamics of action imagery vary with characteristics of the represented agent and action, with imagery unfolding differently for human versus robotic actions as a function of action duration (Viviani et al., 2026).

text.text: The present study therefore contrasts two instructional sets that differ jointly in agency and sensory emphasis: kinesthetic self-imagery and visual object-imagery.
The manipulation is intended to shift the dominant perspective and sensory experience rather than to create completely isolated imagery modalities.
Because agency and sensory emphasis are jointly manipulated, the present design does not isolate these dimensions experimentally.
Rather, it tests the consequences of adopting a self-related, kinesthetic versus object-centered, visually oriented imagery set.
Mental paper folding and mental body rotation provide complementary tests of this distinction.
Mental body rotation requires the transformation of a body representation and therefore provides a relatively strong context for self-related and motor-based processing.

Mental paper folding, in contrast, requires sequential visuospatial transformations but does not inherently specify an acting agent; the paper can be mentally transformed either by imagining oneself performing the folds or by tracking the changing object configuration from an object-centered perspective (Dahm & Sachse, 2025).
text.formatted: Mental paper folding, in contrast, requires sequential visuospatial transformations but does not inherently specify an acting agent; the paper can be mentally transformed either by imagining oneself performing the folds or by tracking the changing object configuration from an object-centered perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Dahm & Sachse, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the two tasks allow us to ask whether the consequences of self-versus object-imagery depend on the representational demands of the task.
If self-related embodied processing is generally advantageous for action imagery, selfimagery should facilitate performance in both tasks.
Alternatively, if imagery representations are flexibly configured according to task demands, the effects of agency should differ between body-centered and object-centered transformations.
A second primary question concerned the relationship between performance across the two tasks.

If self-and object-imagery rely on partially distinct representational configurations, performance should be more strongly associated across tasks when the same imagery perspective is used than when different perspectives are used.
Such agency-congruent associations would provide evidence that the distinction between self-and object-imagery extends beyond task-specific performance effects.
Mental paper folding (Dahm & Draxler, 2022) and mental body rotation (Dahm et al., 2022) provide complementary tests of this distinction.

text.text: We therefore expected vividness to show, at most, weak associations with performance in mental paper folding and mental body rotation.
The instructional manipulation was additionally assessed through task-specific ratings of sensory experience.

We expected self-imagery to increase reports of kinesthetic and self-related sensations, whereas object-imagery should increase reports of visually representing the object or action without an actor (Dahm et al., 2025; Dahm & Rieger, 2023; Guillot et al., 2009; MacIntyre et al., 2013).

text.text: Because the manipulation targets the content and perspective of imagery rather than general imagery ability, overall vividness was not expected to differ substantially between conditions.

Finally, we examined whether performance was related to broader cognitive abilities that are relevant to spatial transformation.

Participants began with either the selfimagery or object-imagery condition.
Within each instruction condition, participants first completed the Mental Paper Folding Task, followed by the Mental Body Rotation Task.

The Mental Paper Folding Task (Dahm & Sachse, 2025; Shepard & Feng, 1972) is a visuospatial reasoning task that assesses the ability to mentally simulate the physical transformation of a two-dimensional object into a three-dimensional object.
text.formatted: The Mental Paper Folding Task <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Dahm & Sachse, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Shepard & Feng, 1972)</ref> is a visuospatial reasoning task that assesses the ability to mentally simulate the physical transformation of a two-dimensional object into a three-dimensional object.

text.text: Participants are shown squares on paper (base grids) that can be folded along the marked lines.
Participants shall imagine to move the paper and align the edges as the folds are made.
At the end of the imagined folding action, they judge as fast and accurately as possible whether two specified edges of the folded paper would overlap.
Participants performed the task in two conditions (counterbalanced order).
In both conditions, they were told that the grid represents a piece of paper that can be folded into a cube.
Two lines in the grid were highlighted (yellow) and participants were asked to evaluate whether these lines would overlap in the cube.
Each trial began with a visually presented countdown from 3 to 1 seconds.
The responses were given by using the 'x' key (no overlap) or the 'm' key (overlap).
This mapping was visually shown on the screen with a red 'X' key on the left and a green 'M' key on the right.
In the kinesthetic self-imagery condition, participants were instructed to focus on the feeling while they imagined folding the paper themselves.

In the visual object-imagery condition, participants were instructed to focus on visual aspects while they imagined that the paper is folded by itself (like an invisible magical hand), i.e., a no-person perspective from the outside (visual imagery without an actor).
To familiarize participants with the task, four familiarization trials were performed in each condition.
The familiarization trials differed from the main block and included feedback about errors and response time.

For the main block, two stimuli were chosen for each potential combination of folds (3 Folds, 4 Folds, 5 Folds), direction changes (Fewer, More), and overlaps (Overlap, No overlap), culminating in a total of 24 trials (as in Dahm & Sachse, 2025).

text.text: The order of the trials was fixed to increase differences in subsequent trials in base grids, direction changes, and number of folds (Dahm & Sachse, 2025).

text.text: To avoid memory-reliance across blocks, object-imagery stimuli were horizontally and vertically mirrored versions of the self-imagery stimuli.
Performance was measured with response times and errors.

The Mental Body Rotation Task (Dahm et al., 2022) engages motor-cognitive interactions by requiring participants map a body image onto their own bodily reference frame after one of them has been mentally rotated.
text.formatted: The Mental Body Rotation Task <ref type="bibr">(Dahm et al., 2022)</ref> engages motor-cognitive interactions by requiring participants map a body image onto their own bodily reference frame after one of them has been mentally rotated.

text.text: This draws upon action imagery, spatial perspective-taking, and limb-specific processing (Dahm & Sachse, 2025).
text.formatted: This draws upon action imagery, spatial perspective-taking, and limb-specific processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Dahm & Sachse, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Participants viewed abstract, gender-neutral schematic figures of human bodies in either front or back perspectives.

Each figure was rotated at one of five angles (45°, 135°, 180°, -135°, -45°; positive indicating clockwise, negative counterclockwise), and one limb (left or right arm or leg) was depicted as raised (total of 40 trials).
The participants' task was to judge as quickly and accurately as possible whether the raised limb was a left or right arm or leg-responding by pressing the 'x' and 'm' key.
In the kinesthetic self-imagery condition, participants were instructed to focus on the feeling while they imagined turning themselves into the depicted position and raising one's own limb.
In the visual object-imagery condition, participants were instructed to focus on visual aspects while they imagined the depicted figure to turn into one's own position and lowering the limb.
To familiarize participants with the task, eight familiarization trials (angle 0°) were performed in each condition.
The order of the items in the main block was fixed.
Items were arranged in a quasi-random sequence to minimize obvious order patterns.
To avoid memory-reliance across blocks, object-imagery stimuli were horizontally and vertically mirrored versions of the self-imagery stimuli.
Performance was measured with response times and error rates.
After each mental paper folding condition and mental body rotation condition, participants rated agency-specific sensory experiences and imagery vividness (see Figure 1).

text.text: For this, participants rated on a scale from 1 (not at all) to 9 (very much) the extent to which they perceived kinesthetic actions of their hands / feeling their own body, visual actions of their hands / seeing their own body, a visual folding of the paper (without hands) / seeing pictured person acting, and acoustic aspects of the folding.
Further, they rated the vividness of mental paper folding / body rotations from 1 (no imagery) to 9 (as vivid as in reality).

The Hagen Matrices Test (Heydasch, 2014) is a non-verbal intelligence test designed to measure fluid intelligence, specifically focusing on abstract spatial reasoning, pattern recognition, and problem-solving abilities.
text.formatted: The Hagen Matrices Test <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Heydasch, 2014)</ref> is a non-verbal intelligence test designed to measure fluid intelligence, specifically focusing on abstract spatial reasoning, pattern recognition, and problem-solving abilities.

text.text: The Hagen Matrices Test presents participants with visual 3x3 matrices in which one element is missing.
The task is to select the correct element from a set of six alternatives that logically completes the pattern, based on rules such as shape transformation, rotation, or progression.
The test consists of 20 items of increasing difficulty.
Participants have maximally 2 minutes to solve each item.
As a score for spatial intelligence, we calculated the percentage of correctly solved items.

The Corsi Task (Corsi, 1973; Kessels et al., 2000) assesses visuospatial span capacity which is the maximum number of sequentially presented spatial locations that an individual can successfully retain, recall, and reproduce in the correct order within short-term.
text.formatted: The Corsi Task <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Corsi, 1973;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kessels et al., 2000)</ref> assesses visuospatial span capacity which is the maximum number of sequentially presented spatial locations that an individual can successfully retain, recall, and reproduce in the correct order within short-term.

text.text: Ten squares (100x100 px) were arranged irregularly on the screen.
Some squares flashed yellow (700 ms) in a certain sequence, and the participants were asked to reproduce the same sequence by clicking on the respective squares.
In the first two trials, two squares flashed yellow.
In the third and fourth trial, three squares flashed yellow.
This procedure was continued, until in the thirteenth and fourteenth trial eight squares flashed yellow.
As a score for visuospatial span capacity, we summed the number of yellow squares from all correctly answered sequences (highest possible number70 = 2*(2+3+4+5+6+7+8)).
The Simon Task was constructed in analogy to the selection of the left and right arrow keys in the Mental Body Rotation Task and the Mental Paper Folding Task.
Each trial (total of 40 trials) started with a fixation dot for 1000 ms.
Then an arrow (1 cm) appeared either at the left (-330 px) or right (+300 px) side of the screen.
The position of the arrow was irrelevant to solve the task, but either congruent or incongruent with the response (Craft & Simon, 1970; Simon & Rudell, 1967).
text.formatted: The position of the arrow was irrelevant to solve the task, but either congruent or incongruent with the response <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Craft & Simon, 1970;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Simon & Rudell, 1967)</ref>.

text.text: Participants were required to press the 'x' key if the arrow indicated towards the left side and to press the 'm' key if the arrow indicated towards the right side.
As a score for visual interference inhibition, we calculated the negative Simon effect (difference in response times between congruent and incongruent trials).
As a manipulation check, comparisons between self-imagery and objectimagery were conducted using t-tests with Holm adjusted pairwise comparisons.
We examined participants' response times and errors separately in mental paper folding and mental body rotations to assess their sensitivity to changes in imagery strategy.
Additionally, we exploratively examined potential practice or carryover effects resulting from the within-subjects design.

To test whether the patterns observed in the data distributions reflected an interaction between Instruction and Block, indicating possible carryover effects, we fitted separate models for mental paper folding and mental body rotations.

Linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) were used for log-transformed response times from correct trials, and generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) with a binomial distribution and a logit link function were used for trial-level errors.
For mental paper folding, Folds and Direction Changes (both grand-mean centered) were included as covariates.
For mental body rotations, Limb, Perspective (effect-coded), and Rotation (absolute values divided by 100 to ensure numerical stability) served as covariates.
In all models, Participant was included as a random intercept, and Instruction (self-vs. object-imagery) and Block (first vs. second) were entered as effectcoded fixed effects.
We compared models including and excluding the Instruction × Block interaction (see Table 1).

text.text: There was a small correlation of mental body rotation response times during self-imagery with external visual imagery and visual interference inhibition.
Further, there were small correlations of mental body rotation error rates with self-rated internal visual imagery, both, when using self-imagery and object-imagery.
In mental paper folding error rates using object-imagery, there were small correlations with spatial intelligence and visuospatial span capacity.
Our study compared effects of kinesthetic self-imagery and visual objectimagery instructions in mental paper folding and mental body rotations.
Participants reported a stronger feeling of the hands with kinesthetic self-imagery instructions than visual object-imagery instructions, aligning with the manipulation.
In mental paper folding, responses were faster in object-imagery than self-imagery, which was modified by an interaction with the order of imagery instructions.
In mental body rotations in contrast, responses were slower in object-imagery than in self-imagery.
However, in both, mental paper folding and mental body rotations, errors did not significantly differ between self-imagery and object-imagery.
Our findings provide evidence that instructions can modulate processing efficiency, suggesting partially dissociable mechanisms.
Correlations with self-reported vividness of movement imagery, inhibitory control, spatial intelligence, and visuospatial span capacity, were small or close to zero.
Self-ratings following mental paper folding confirmed that instructional manipulations successfully evoked distinct imagery experiences.

Self-imagery instructions elicited higher ratings for feeling the own hands, seeing the own hands, and hearing the paper, whereas object-imagery instructions elicited higher ratings for seeing the paper without hands.
Vividness ratings did not differ significantly between conditions, suggesting comparable subjective clarity of imagery across agency instructions.

Similarly, in mental body rotations, self-imagery instructions elicited higher ratings for feeling the own body and seeing the own body, while object-imagery instructions elicited higher ratings for seeing an action in the picture.
Again, vividness did not differ significantly between agency instructions.

These findings align with previous work demonstrating that imagery instructions selectively modulate sensory-motor components of imagery experience without necessarily affecting overall vividness (Guillot et al., 2009; MacIntyre et al., 2013).
text.formatted: These findings align with previous work demonstrating that imagery instructions selectively modulate sensory-motor components of imagery experience without necessarily affecting overall vividness <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Guillot et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">MacIntyre et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: In mental paper folding, response times and errors increased significantly with the number of folds and direction changes, consistent with the notion that folding engages sequential spatial transformations and cumulative working memory demands (Harris et al., 2013).
text.formatted: In mental paper folding, response times and errors increased significantly with the number of folds and direction changes, consistent with the notion that folding engages sequential spatial transformations and cumulative working memory demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Harris et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: This pattern replicates earlier findings showing that response time in mental paper folding increases with the number of folds, not only in execution (Dahm & Sachse, 2025), but also in imagery (Dahm & Draxler, 2022; Dahm & Sachse, 2025).
text.formatted: This pattern replicates earlier findings showing that response time in mental paper folding increases with the number of folds, not only in execution <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Dahm & Sachse, 2025)</ref>, but also in imagery <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Dahm & Draxler, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Dahm & Sachse, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, more complex folding sequences require more cognitive resources.
This reinforces the interpretation of mental paper folding as a sequential transformation task relying on cumulative representational updating.

Alternatively, more folds may increase the probability of error occurrences which can either materialize in accuracy failure or in an increased response time (if participants repeat the step or start the mental folding from the beginning to correct the error).
In mental body rotations, responses were faster and more accurate for smaller rotation angles, for back-view compared to front-view perspectives, and for hand compared to foot stimuli.

These findings replicate previous research (Dahm et al., 2022), showing that leg stimuli were more challenging than arm stimuli, particularly in rotated positions, suggesting that distinguishing between left and right legs is more difficult than for arms.
text.formatted: These findings replicate previous research <ref type="bibr">(Dahm et al., 2022)</ref>, showing that leg stimuli were more challenging than arm stimuli, particularly in rotated positions, suggesting that distinguishing between left and right legs is more difficult than for arms.

text.text: Further, the front-view perspective requires a vertical rotation in the mind which slows down responses (Dahm et al., 2022; Habacha et al., 2017; Kaltner et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Further, the front-view perspective requires a vertical rotation in the mind which slows down responses <ref type="bibr">(Dahm et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Habacha et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Kaltner et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Across both tasks, performance improved from the first to the second block, indicating reliable practice-related gains.

Such improvements are consistent with previous findings showing that repeated engagement with mental rotation and spatial transformation tasks leads to faster and more efficient processing, even over relatively short timescales (Dahm & Draxler, 2022; Shepard & Metzler, 1971; Wohlschläger & Wohlschläger, 1998).
text.formatted: Such improvements are consistent with previous findings showing that repeated engagement with mental rotation and spatial transformation tasks leads to faster and more efficient processing, even over relatively short timescales <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Dahm & Draxler, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Shepard & Metzler, 1971;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Wohlschläger & Wohlschläger, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: From a cognitive perspective, these gains likely reflect increasing familiarity with stimulus structures and task requirements, as well as the refinement of imagery strategies with practice (Onishi et al., 2025).
text.formatted: From a cognitive perspective, these gains likely reflect increasing familiarity with stimulus structures and task requirements, as well as the refinement of imagery strategies with practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Onishi et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Such rapid improvements suggest flexible adaptation of representational strategies rather than structural changes in imagery ability.

The significantly stronger practice effect after self-imagery than after objectimagery for response times in mental paper folding is consistent with the instructions influencing subsequent processing.
Here, performance improvement was greater when switching from self-imagery to object-imagery than vice versa.

Participants who used self-imagery in Block 1 may have continued to rely, at least partially, on selfreferential imagery processes during Block 2 when instructed to use object-imagery, thereby retaining the associated performance advantages.
Participants who began with object-imagery, by contrast, likely did not spontaneously engage in self-imagery when instructed to use object-imagery.
This asymmetry suggests that self-referential representations can persist even when task demands change.

We did not observe such a carryover-effect in mental body rotations, likely indicating that body-related stimuli in the MBRT elicited motor-related processing during imagery rather automatically (e.g., through perspective taking; Moreno-Verdú, Waltzing, McAteer, et al., 2025), and thus largely independent of explicit instruction, whereas the non-body stimuli in mental paper folding did not.

text.text: Mental paper folding stimuli do not inherently depict an actor and can be solved with an object-centered visuospatial imagery strategy (Dahm & Sachse, 2025).
text.formatted: Mental paper folding stimuli do not inherently depict an actor and can be solved with an object-centered visuospatial imagery strategy <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Dahm & Sachse, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Motor involvement may therefore be less likely to arise spontaneously in mental paper folding unless it is explicitly induced by instruction.
This interpretation aligns with previous prior work showing that rotation of body-related stimuli, but not rotation of objects, activates motor areas and premotor areas (Kosslyn et al., 1998).
text.formatted: This interpretation aligns with previous prior work showing that rotation of body-related stimuli, but not rotation of objects, activates motor areas and premotor areas <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Kosslyn et al., 1998)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, mental rotation of hand stimuli increased motor-cortical involvement during subsequent mental rotation with abstract, non-body stimuli, whereas prior rotation of abstract objects did not produce the same effect (Wraga et al., 2003).
text.formatted: Similarly, mental rotation of hand stimuli increased motor-cortical involvement during subsequent mental rotation with abstract, non-body stimuli, whereas prior rotation of abstract objects did not produce the same effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Wraga et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Response times were more strongly correlated across tasks when imagery instructions matched than when they differed.

This descriptive pattern is consistent with shared instruction-related contributions to processing speed, potentially reflecting individual differences in the use of self-related kinesthetic or object-based visual strategies.
However, error rate correlations did not show a consistent corresponding pattern.
Moreover, shared temporal context and order effects provide alternative explanations for the response time pattern.
These findings therefore suggest possible instruction-specific commonalities across tasks but do not establish distinct representational systems.
Studies have demonstrated that imagery can span multiple sensory modalities (Floridou et al., 2022) supporting the idea of a multimodal representation system (Krüger et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Studies have demonstrated that imagery can span multiple sensory modalities <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Floridou et al., 2022)</ref> supporting the idea of a multimodal representation system <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Krüger et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, imagery instruction did not influence the occurrence of errors.
This supports the view that imagery is inherently multimodal, such that imagery engages a mixture of modalities rather than a purely isolated form (Dahm et al., 2025; Dahm & Rieger, 2023).
text.formatted: This supports the view that imagery is inherently multimodal, such that imagery engages a mixture of modalities rather than a purely isolated form <ref type="bibr">(Dahm et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Dahm & Rieger, 2023</ref>).

text.text: Yet, self-reports were expectably aligned towards the instructed agency and modality.
Regarding imagery speed, response times were longer in object-imagery than in self-imagery in mental body rotations.
In contrast, response times were shorter in object-imagery than self-imagery in mental paper folding.

Therefore, we conclude that mental body rotations benefit from embodied cognition that involves oneself as an actor, whereas mental paper folding becomes more complex by including the own person perspective and kinesthetic aspects.
Hence, as assumed previously (Dahm & Sachse, 2025) to effectively solve mental paper folding, a first person perspective is not necessary.
text.formatted: Hence, as assumed previously <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Dahm & Sachse, 2025)</ref> to effectively solve mental paper folding, a first person perspective is not necessary.

text.text: Regarding mental body rotations however, agency as oneself benefits response speed.
This goes in line with studies showing that people with aphantasia do not make more errors than people without aphantasia, but they do show longer response times (Kay et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This goes in line with studies showing that people with aphantasia do not make more errors than people without aphantasia, but they do show longer response times <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Kay et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these findings indicate a task-dependent advantage of embodied processing, rather than a general superiority of self-imagery.

Performance in both tasks did not correlate meaningfully with vividness scores from the Vividness of Movement Imagery Questionnaire, reinforcing previous observations that self-report imagery measures often fail to predict behavioral performance (Czilczer, Sachse, et al., 2026; Moreau et al., 2010; Suggate, 2024).

text.text: This dissociation challenges the assumption that vividness reflects functional efficiency in imagery-based cognition and underscores the importance of combining both objective, performance-based measures, and subjective, self-report measures, when assessing imagery ability (Czilczer, Moreno-Verdú, et al., 2026; Dahm, 2020).

Such correlations with visuospatial span capacity and spatial intelligence were not observed for mental body rotations, yet, more interference inhibition was weakly associated with shorter response times using self-imagery.

Together, these results provide further support for the view that mental paper folding requires more abstract object-imagery abilities, whereas mental body rotations require own-body centered self-imagery abilities (Steggemann et al., 2011).

text.text: This study collected data from a range of behavioral tasks, and therefore we decided to reduce the number of trials collected from each task to minimize fatigue and inattention, particularly because data was collected remotely.
This represents a limitation, as the number of trials is an important factor for task reliability (Zorowitz & Niv, 2023).
text.formatted: This represents a limitation, as the number of trials is an important factor for task reliability <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Zorowitz & Niv, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, our study collected data from a sample substantially larger than previously achieved.
Therefore, the group-level estimates are more robust to trial-level noise (Cohen, 2013).
text.formatted: Therefore, the group-level estimates are more robust to trial-level noise <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Cohen, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Neurophysiological and behavioral evidence indicates that kinesthetic and visual imagery can evoke distinct patterns of activation and classification (Chholak et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Neurophysiological and behavioral evidence indicates that kinesthetic and visual imagery can evoke distinct patterns of activation and classification <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Chholak et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Yang et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Still, imagery may leave short-lived sensory traces that bias subsequent perception (Pearson et al., 2008), a mechanism that may provoke carry-over effects in the absence of an explicit washout period.
text.formatted: Still, imagery may leave short-lived sensory traces that bias subsequent perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Pearson et al., 2008)</ref>, a mechanism that may provoke carry-over effects in the absence of an explicit washout period.

text.text: Further, one may question whether participants engaged in genuinely distinct processes during selfimagery and object-imagery, particularly given the absence of a washout period between conditions.

Although participants reported performing different forms of imagery, such reports could reflect the intention to comply with instructions rather than true differences in simulation strategies (Guillot & Collet, 2005).
text.formatted: Although participants reported performing different forms of imagery, such reports could reflect the intention to comply with instructions rather than true differences in simulation strategies <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Guillot & Collet, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, instructions were not directly followed by the ratings.
Participants first performed all trials of the task, and reported what they had been doing after completing the task.
Body-related stimuli in behavioral tasks may recruit motor-related processing during imagery relatively automatically and thus largely independently of explicit instruction.

By contrast, non-body stimuli may not recruit motor-related processing unless it is induced by instruction, and may instead promote a purely visuospatial, non-action-specific strategy (Kosslyn et al., 1998).
text.formatted: By contrast, non-body stimuli may not recruit motor-related processing unless it is induced by instruction, and may instead promote a purely visuospatial, non-action-specific strategy <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Kosslyn et al., 1998)</ref>.

text.text: This distinction is critical when the aim is to measure action imagery ability specifically, because instructions can shape the processing of the stimuli.
In addition, strategy-related carryover effects may occur across tasks, such that strategies adopted in earlier tasks influence performance in later tasks (Wraga et al., 2003).
text.formatted: In addition, strategy-related carryover effects may occur across tasks, such that strategies adopted in earlier tasks influence performance in later tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Wraga et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, when using a battery of behavioral tasks (Czilczer, Moreno-Verdú, et al., 2026; Moreno-Verdú, Waltzing, Caenegem, et al., 2025), researchers should consider not only imagery instructions (Moreno-Verdú et al., 2024) but also task order and prior task context to improve interpretability and comparability across studies.

text.text: Overall, the present findings refine current accounts of action imagery by demonstrating that agency and modality can modulate imagery processing.
In our study, imagery instructions influenced response times, but not error rates, providing no clear evidence of a speed-accuracy trade-off.

The medium cross-task response time correlations under congruent imagery instructions suggest possible instruction-specific commonalities in processing across mental paper folding and mental body rotation.

While this is consistent with evidence for differential recruitment of motor and visuospatial systems (Guillot et al., 2009; Kosslyn et al., 2001), inconsistent correlations for error rates limit conclusions about distinct imagery processes.
text.formatted: While this is consistent with evidence for differential recruitment of motor and visuospatial systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Guillot et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Kosslyn et al., 2001)</ref>, inconsistent correlations for error rates limit conclusions about distinct imagery processes.

text.text: At the same time, the lack of strong associations with self-reported vividness suggests that subjective imagery experience and objective performance capture dissociable components of imagery ability.

The present findings are consistent with a flexible account of imagery in which the contribution of self-related kinesthetic and objectcentered visual processing varies with task demands and imagery instructions.
One possible interpretation is that these processing modes draw on different configurations of a partially shared simulation system.
Alternatively, the tasks may be solved through partly distinct motor and visuospatial strategies.
Self-related processing may therefore be advantageous in some task contexts, while explicit self-imagery instructions are not necessary for successful performance across these tasks.

This perspective offers a framework for investigating when object-centered transformations involve action simulations and how perceptual and motor representations contribute to imagery under different task and instructional conditions.
